account:
It is day one, about 08:26, and I am in my office with the secretary and a visiting neighbour. I reviewed all four office books this morning and returned them to the appointments chest. Today's business is the ten o'clock mill grain inspection, lunch at home, council letters at thirteen, tea at the neighbour's east-bank cottage at fifteen, office at sixteen-thirty, and the great-hall lighting inspection at eighteen before going home at nineteen.

The most unusual report is a possible grain shortage. The secretary says she overheard the builder discussing it yesterday and seeking the miller's assistance, mentioning forty-six hay bales. She has not verified either the quantity or its circumstances, so I do not yet know whether this is an actual shortage, a proposed supply arrangement, or something else. I intend to ask the miller at the inspection rather than spread it as established news.

The builder has installed eight lanterns in the great hall and requested today's eighteen-hundred inspection. I approved it yesterday, funded a replacement writable appointment book when the signed original could not be amended, and have now read the updated entry. The builder reaffirmed the meeting this morning and plans to accompany me into the hall. As far as I know, this is to review the hall lighting; I have seen no evidence of another purpose.

Yesterday's vague talk of bridge or port changes remains unconfirmed. Both secretary and builder reported no concrete proposal, and the builder said he had no such works planned. The neighbour now reports that the baker said yesterday's bread arrangements went smoothly and that fresh bread is being baked today. I do not know the details of those arrangements. The neighbour has also reconfirmed our usual three o'clock tea. No new correspondence has reached the secretary. For now, normal appointments continue, with grain stocks the main matter needing verification.
